Class 9 note - Siddharth (class teacher), Tuesday
When the class voted to hold our charity bake sale at the mall on Saturday, almost every hand went up. Bhavna's went halfway, then down. She raised an eyebrow and said, "Maybe... I'm not sure."
A few students groaned. Someone said, "Don't spoil it."
I asked the class to let her speak. She said, slowly, "Doesn't the mall need permission? And who's bringing the oven? And if it rains, how do we get the cakes there?"
Three good questions. Nobody had thought of any of them.
Her doubt came from careful thinking, not from being negative. I told the class so. We made a list of what we'd need to check.
Bhavna volunteered to phone the mall office. On Thursday she told us they needed a letter from the school, and it took two days, so we moved the sale to the following week.

qa.a: Three good questions.

Maria wants us both to try out for the district basketball team on Saturday. She's so excited. I said, "Maybe," and changed the subject.
Truth: I'm scared. Not of the game. Of the trial. Of standing in front of coaches I don't know and missing every shot. Of Maria getting in and me not.

That made it smaller.
I think I'm going. Still scared. But the maybe is more of a yes now.
- Nazia

Kishore, you asked how my tutoring thing went. So, I'm Aadhya, and every Saturday I help Class 6 kids with maths at the community centre.
First week, there was this boy, Ronak, who frowned the whole time. Arms crossed, eyes narrowed. I thought, great, he's bored. He hates me. So I talked faster to get it over with.
Next week, same frown. So I stopped and just asked, "Ronak, are you bored, or is something confusing?"
He looked shocked. "Confusing! The fractions part. I didn't want to say."
I'd read his frown completely wrong. It was concentration, and confusion. Not boredom at all.
Meanwhile the girl next to him, who smiled and nodded the whole time? She'd understood nothing either. Her smile was politeness.
So now I don't trust faces. I ask one question every ten minutes. "Still with me?"

I'm Mohit, and I watched Sunaina present her coding project to our class on Friday. She was explaining loops, really fast, clicking through slides.
She kept looking at the back row. Three boys were leaning back, chins on hands, eyes half closed. I saw her face drop. She sped up even more. I guessed she thought they were bored.

At the end, Sunaina said, a bit flatly, "Any questions? Probably not."
The frowning boy put his hand up. "Can you go back to the second loop? I didn't get where it stops."
Sunaina looked surprised. Then she smiled and went back. Three more hands went up after that.

I remember exactly where I was when Papa told us. The dining table, Sunday lunch, rajma going cold. "We're moving to Toronto in August. My company is transferring me."
I froze with the spoon halfway to my mouth. I couldn't breathe properly. My ears were ringing. My brother was asking questions and I heard nothing.
Toronto. August. My school, my friends, Mahima.
I left the table and walked to the park without saying anything.
Mahima found me there an hour later; Mumma had called her. She didn't say, "It'll be exciting!" She sat on the swing next to mine and didn't speak for a long time.
Finally I said, "I can't even feel anything yet."
She said, "That's okay. You don't have to yet."
It took me days to feel it. Some of it was sad. Later, some of it was exciting. But that first hour, I needed quiet.
- Mehak

The national camp selections came by email during practice. I read out the names. When I said "Reena Tiwari," Reena gasped out loud and froze mid-stretch. Her hands went to her face. She didn't move for several seconds.
Her teammates started cheering and rushing towards her. I could see she wasn't ready. Her eyes were huge and she was breathing fast.
I asked them to give her a minute and let her sit on the bench. I sat nearby without talking.
After a minute she started to cry. Then laugh. She said, "I didn't even think I'd be shortlisted. I told my mother not to hope."
Then she let the team hug her.

In the small town of Nabha, Shankar noticed that his daughter Hansa had gone quiet. After school she lay on the charpai with her phone, scrolling without really looking. When he asked about her day, she said, "Fine." Dinner? "Okay." Tuition? "Hmm."
His brother said, "She's become rude. Take the phone away."

"You're hurt."

Shankar nodded. "Tell me about her."
Hansa talked until the tea went cold.

I'm Hrithik, and I was standing next to Sharmila when the drama club cast list went up. She'd auditioned for the lead. The lead went to someone else. Sharmila got "Villager 3."
Everyone around us was squealing or groaning. Sharmila just looked at the list. Her face was completely blank. No frown, no sigh.
"Cool," she said. "Villagers are fun."
I honestly couldn't tell what she felt. Maybe she didn't care. Maybe she did.
At lunch she was her normal self, joking. But she didn't eat her paratha.
After school I walked with her to the gate. I didn't ask about the list in front of anyone. I just said, "If you ever want to talk about the audition, I'm around. Or not. Either's fine."
She kept walking. Then, at the gate: "I practised every night for a month." Her voice cracked a little.
"I know," I said. "I heard you through the wall."

qa.a: Sharmila got "Villager 3."

qa.q: What might Sharmila have been feeling behind her blank face?
qa.a: Sharmila was probably hurt and disappointed after practising for a month, but kept a blank face to protect her privacy in front of peers.

qa.a: Hrithik waited until they were away from others and offered to listen without pressure, saying either choice was fine.

qa.q: How might the other students have read Sharmila's reaction?
qa.a: They might have thought she didn't care about the lead, since her face and words showed nothing.

Ojas, you're wondering why your friend didn't smile when he won? Let your Chinmay Ajoba tell you about the day I kept my face like a stone.
I was fifteen. The headmaster read the scholarship results at assembly. My name was there. My elder brother's wasn't. He'd tried for two years.
I felt like shouting with joy. But he was standing three rows behind me. So I kept my face completely still. No smile. When friends congratulated me, I just nodded.
That night, I couldn't sleep. I was so happy and felt so guilty for being happy.
My grandmother noticed I'd been silent all evening. She called me to the verandah. "Chinmay, your face has been shut all day. Is it joy or sadness you're hiding?"
I said, "Both." And I finally let it out.
She held my hand and said, "You can be happy and kind at the same time."

Gautam, you've gone red again, haven't you? Come here. Your Hrithik Mama was worse, I promise.
At fifteen I blushed at everything. Ordering tea. Answering roll call. Once a girl just asked me the time and I turned the colour of a tomato. The more I thought "don't go red," the redder I went.
I started skipping class presentations. I pretended to be sick on sports day.

"At the ball."
"Not at the crowd?"
"No."
"Then when you talk, look at the ball. The words. The person. Not at your own face. And breathe out slowly, like before a big shot."
I tried it. Still went red sometimes. But I stopped hiding. And, Gautam, most people never noticed. They were busy worrying about themselves.

"Did she see me go red?" Lokesh whispered.

Gurpreet, you won't mind me telling this on the podcast, right? Okay. I'm Nikita, and last year I completely misread my best friend's tears.
Gurpreet opened the scholarship email in the library. She read it, and tears started pouring down her face. She put her head on the desk.
I panicked. I thought, she didn't get it. I started saying, "It's okay, there are other scholarships, you're still brilliant..."
She lifted her head. "Nikita. I got it."

I felt so silly. I'd been comforting her for the wrong thing.
Now, when someone cries, I just sit down next to them and ask, "Happy tears, sad tears, or some other tears?" And I wait.

Angry tears. I'd have guessed wrong.

qa.a: Wasim's tears showed fury and frustration at being mocked when he had studied hard, not sadness.
